n: Another message: a lament for Tyre, pictured as a magnificent merchant ship. Revelation 18 later echoes this chapter in its lament for “Babylon.”

f.w: The word of the LORD came again unto me

n: Ezekiel is to sing a funeral song for Tyre—while she is still thriving.
Tyre sits at the gateway to the sea, trading with many coastlands. She boasts, “I am perfect in beauty.” Pride is the core of her sin.
Her territory is the sea, and her builders made her beautiful—a perfect ship.

f.w: Thy borders are in the midst of the seas
f.g: Tyre’s island setting made her like a ship anchored offshore.

n: Her planks came from fir (juniper) trees of Mount Hermon and her mast from a cedar of Lebanon.

f.g: The Amorite name for Mount Hermon.

n: Her oars were of Bashan oak; her deck was cypress inlaid with ivory from Cyprus.

f.g: A fertile region east of the Sea of Galilee, famous for oaks.
Kittim—Cyprus and the western coastlands.

n: Her sail was embroidered Egyptian linen; her awnings were blue and purple from Elishah (likely Cyprus).

f.g: Probably Alashiya, an ancient name for Cyprus.

n: Men of Sidon and Arvad, neighboring Phoenician cities, were her rowers; Tyre’s own experts were her captains.

f.g: Sidon and Arvad, Phoenician ports north of Tyre.

n: Veteran craftsmen of Gebal (Byblos) sealed her seams, and sailors from every ship came to trade with her.

f.g: Byblos, an ancient Phoenician city known for shipbuilding.
Workers who sealed a ship’s seams against leaks.

n: Mercenaries from Persia, Lud, and Put served in her army, hanging their shields on her walls as decoration.

f.w: Persia and of Lud and of Phut
f.g: Persia, Lydia (in Asia Minor), and Put (Libya)—soldiers hired from distant lands.

n: Men of Arvad and Gammad guarded her walls and towers, their shields adding to her splendor.

f.g: An unknown people—perhaps “valorous men.”

n: Verses 12–24 list Tyre’s trading partners like a ship’s cargo manifest. Tarshish, far to the west (possibly Spain), traded silver, iron, tin, and lead.

f.g: A distant western port, often identified with Tartessus in Spain.

n: Greece (Javan), Tubal, and Meshech in Asia Minor traded slaves and bronze vessels.

f.g: Ionian Greeks and peoples of Anatolia.
Slaves—condemned elsewhere in scripture.

n: Beth-togarmah (in Armenia) supplied horses, war horses, and mules.

f.g: A region in eastern Anatolia/Armenia.

n: Dedan and many coastlands brought ivory tusks and ebony as payment.

f.g: Elephant tusks and black hardwood from Africa or India.

n: Aram (Syria)—or perhaps Edom—traded gems, purple fabric, embroidery, linen, coral, and rubies.

f.g: Many manuscripts read “Edom.”
Possibly ruby.

n: Judah and Israel supplied agricultural goods: wheat, millet (or pastries), honey, oil, and balm.

f.g: An Ammonite town.
Unknown; perhaps a kind of cake or millet.

n: Damascus traded wine from Helbon and white wool.

f.g: A region north of Damascus famous for wine.

n: Others brought wrought iron and spices like cassia and calamus.

f.g: Fragrant spices used in perfumes and holy anointing oil.

n: Dedan supplied saddle blankets for riding.

f.g: Saddlecloths.

n: Arabia and the princes of Kedar traded lambs, rams, and goats.

f.g: A powerful Arabian tribe descended from Ishmael.

n: Sheba and Raamah in southern Arabia brought the finest spices, precious stones, and gold.

f.g: A wealthy kingdom in southwest Arabia (modern Yemen).

n: Mesopotamian cities—Haran, Canneh, Eden, Asshur, and Chilmad—also traded with her.

f.g: The city where Abraham once lived.

n: They supplied fine garments, blue and embroidered cloth, and colorful carpets tied with cords.

f.g: Multicolored carpets or trunks of fine clothing.

n: Ships of Tarshish carried her goods; she was loaded with cargo and glorious in the heart of the seas.

f.g: Large ocean-going merchant ships.

n: But her rowers took her into deep water, and the east wind wrecked her. Babylon, from the east, is the storm.

f.w: the east wind hath broken thee

n: Everything—cargo, crew, captains, carpenters, traders, and soldiers—sinks with her on the day of her ruin.

f.w: shall fall into the midst of the seas

n: The shorelands shake at the cries of her sailors.

f.g: Pasturelands or coastlands.

n: Sailors and captains from every ship abandon their vessels and stand on shore.
They cry bitterly, throw dust on their heads, and roll in ashes.

f.w: cast up dust upon their heads

n: They shave their heads, wear sackcloth, and weep with anguish.

f.g: Shaving the head was a mourning custom.

n: They lament: “Who was ever like Tyre, now silent in the sea?”
Her trade satisfied many peoples and enriched kings throughout the world.

f.w: thou didst enrich the kings of the earth

n: Now she lies wrecked in the deep with all her goods and crew.

f.g: Shipwrecked.

n: Coastland peoples are horrified, and their kings shudder in fear.

f.g: Appalled.

n: Merchants hiss in shock. Tyre has come to a horrible end and will be no more—showing how quickly worldly wealth and pride can collapse.

f.g: A sound of astonishment or scorn.
